## The question

I still type some version of "create a measure that ranks customers." It feels finished.

An assistant can hand back DAX, the formula language in Power BI (Microsoft's reporting product), in a single reply. The semantic model under the report, where those measures live, will then calculate a rank, and the rank still will not say who is allowed to compete.

Alberto Ferrari posted [Understanding DAX contracts when using AI](https://www.sqlbi.com/tv/understanding-dax-contracts-when-using-ai/) this week, on a video page that is only a note. I read the [article](https://www.sqlbi.com/articles/understanding-dax-contracts-when-using-ai/) he and Marco Russo published with it on 5 October 2026. I did not watch the video.

Their opening claim is the one I am keeping. An AI-written model is usable once the contract exists, with the measure written after it. I am dropping their last sentence, the one that finds no drawbacks. A written rule can still name the wrong race. Follow that rule without a second look, and a meeting will treat the wrong race as finished work.

## What has to be true before a rank exists

In their definition, a contract is text that states how one semantic model is allowed to compute, and several measures can share it. I use a shorter test. Can a colleague argue with the choices that change the number without opening the formula?

Their demo refuses the obvious prompt. They ask the assistant what has to be settled before any DAX is written. The questions that move a rank are who competes, which filters touch sales and which are ignored, whether the largest amount is rank 1, how a tie breaks, whether a customer with no sales or with negative sales stays in, whether identity is the key or the name on the visual, and what a total shows when the row is not one customer.

The contract they save is odd on purpose. A customer competes with everyone who bought from the first sale on record through the end of the period shown. First sale on 1 January 2026 and the report on March 2026 means a cohort through 31 March. Miss that window and the customer drops out. A buyer from an earlier month, with no purchase in the month on the report, still takes a place in the order. Other filters still apply, while a filter on the customer table does not. Cumulative sales set the order, highest first, and CustomerKey ascending breaks a tie so the smaller key wins. Names can appear on the matrix, but identity stays on the key. If the context holds more than one customer, including a name that maps to several keys, the measure returns blank.

Say a sales manager hears March and means invoices booked that month. This contract means a running total through 31 March, scored against people who may have bought nothing in March. I would not paste that cohort into a board pack. I would keep it only after the person who owns the target signs the sentence. The model does not negotiate. It ranks the people the text names.

They request the measure only once the contract has been saved, shown back, and patched. The DAX insists on one customer key, removes customer filters, accumulates sales through the last visible date, and counts how many customers sit ahead. They note that RANK might do the same job faster. In the matrix they publish, Karen Westbrook is first in 2023 and third in 2024 because newer customers bought more than she did. That result is theirs. I have not reproduced it.

## A clean contract can still be the wrong call

The article already says the measure is imperfect and that checking it sits outside the piece. The conclusion still says that, to their knowledge so far, a contract has no drawbacks. I reject the conclusion. A precise file that describes a bad cohort will be implemented without complaint, and the meeting will treat the number as sourced.

Blank on a repeated name refuses to invent one rank for two keys, and then it goes quiet. Unless someone is assigned to that blank, the collision never surfaces in the review.

One rewritten example also cannot tell me how often an assistant's contract drifts away from the sentences a person typed. Russo and Ferrari show a clearer rewrite and say the author should read it back. That habit is not proof the drift is usually harmless. Until I do the read-back on a model I maintain, "the agent cleaned it up" stays unverified.

On Orbit, the public site where an essay like this gets published, an assistant may write the draft and a person still has to approve it. I want that split on a ranking measure: the formula may sit in the model, and a file has to remain the copy a colleague can mark up.

On Monday that file sits beside the model. It names the cohort, the filters the rank ignores, the tie break, and the result when the row is not one customer. I change the file before I ask for new DAX. Then I calculate one customer by hand, using only that file. If I have to open the formula to decide whether a historical buyer with no sales this month belongs, the contract is unfinished. A chat transcript does not count as the file. The next edit will land in the measure, and the written rule will be stale.

What stays broken is the review. Someone still has to explain a rank that moved, and they cannot, if the reason was never stored.

## Takeaway

I will not ask for a ranking measure until a contract names who competes, which filters do not count, how a tie breaks, and what a repeated name returns. I change that contract before I change the formula. One customer I can calculate by hand has to match, or the measure stays out of any report a team will use. No file beside the model, no ship.
